name: Inequity aversion
statement: People will pay to avoid unequal payoffs, turning down money rather than accept a split that leaves them far behind the person they are dealing with.
meaning: Three claims travel under this name and they need separating. The first is a behavioural regularity: responders in bargaining experiments turn down small offers, which costs them money. The second is a formal model of preference. Fehr and Schmidt write utility as material payoff minus a penalty for the gap between own and others' payoffs, weighting the case of falling behind more heavily than the case of getting ahead. They call it self-centred inequity aversion, meaning a person cares about the gap between themselves and others rather than about inequality among third parties. Bolton and Ockenfels published a related model a year later, built on relative payoff standing rather than pairwise gaps. The third claim is comparative: that other animals share the aversion and refuse a poor reward when a neighbour gets a better one for the same work. The three stand or fall separately, and the evidence for them is of different quality.

origin.who: Ernst Fehr and Klaus M. Schmidt
origin.note: Their paper is "A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation", 114(3), 817-868. It supplied the name and the algebra, citing Adams among earlier writers on equity and citing Loewenstein, Thompson and Bazerman for the asymmetry between falling behind and getting ahead. Gary Bolton and Axel Ockenfels reached a related model independently in the American Economic Review in 2000. The experimental base both were built on starts with Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze's ultimatum game in 1982.

evidence: Oosterbeek, Sloof and van de Kuilen pooled 37 papers reporting 75 ultimatum-game results. Proposers offered 40% of the pie on average, and 16% of offers were rejected, with rejection falling as the pie grew and as the offered share rose. Fehr and Schmidt fitted their model to ultimatum data with a discrete distribution of two parameters: an envy weight of 0 for 30% of subjects, 0.5 for 30%, 1 for 30% and 4 for 10%, and a guilt weight of 0 for 30%, 0.25 for 30% and 0.6 for 40%. An envy weight of 1 means giving up a dollar to cut the opponent's payoff by two. Henrich and colleagues took the game to 15 small-scale societies. Group mean offers ran from 26% to 58%, against the 40% to 50% typical of student samples, and modal offers from 15% to 50%. Machiguenga horticulturalists in Peru had a mean of 0.26 and modes at 0.15 and 0.25, and their responders rejected a single offer although more than 75% of offers were below 30% of the pie. Lamalera whalers in Indonesia had a mean of 0.57, and 63% of proposers split the pie evenly. Hadza foragers rejected 24% of all offers and nine of the 21 offers at or below 20%. The Au and Gnau of Papua New Guinea rejected offers above 50% about as often as offers below it. Brosnan and de Waal reported in 2003 that brown capuchins refused to trade a token for cucumber once a neighbour received a grape for the same token, which is the result the popular video shows.

replication.headline: People really do reject low offers, at 16% pooled across 37 ultimatum papers, but no inequity effect survives a meta-analysis of 23 animal studies.
replication.detail: The two literatures pull apart. On the human side Oosterbeek, Sloof and van de Kuilen found a 16% rejection rate across 75 results from 37 papers, and the behavioural pattern is not in dispute. On the animal side Ritov, Völter, Raihani and Engelmann obtained the primary data behind 23 accept/reject studies, covering 302 subjects, 60,430 observations and 18 species. The coefficient for the inequity condition was 0.257, with a bootstrapped 95% interval running from -0.029 to 0.543 and p = 0.0923. No pre-registered subset reached p < 0.05: capuchin monkeys gave 0.375 with an interval of -0.294 to 0.979, and chimpanzees gave -0.075 with an interval of -0.640 to 0.514. The disappointment condition, where a better reward is shown without a partner being favoured, gave 0.513 with an interval of 0.108 to 0.955 and p = 0.0339. Engelmann, Clift, Herrmann and Tomasello had shown the same thing directly in nine chimpanzees, who refused food from a human experimenter on 26.1% of trials and from a machine on 2.4%, and who refused most often when no partner was present at all.

study.cite: Ritov, O., Völter, C. J., Raihani, N. J., & Engelmann, J. M. (2024). No evidence for inequity aversion in non-human animals: a meta-analysis of accept/reject paradigms. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 291(2035), 20241452.

limits: The animal meta-analysis covers accept/reject tasks only. Its authors approached 30 eligible publications and received data for 23, and they dropped conditions in which the subject faced no effortful task, so the synthesis is narrower than the literature it reviews. On the model side, Binmore and Shaked argue that ultimatum data cannot pin the Fehr-Schmidt parameters down at all: a proposer who offers half the pie tells you only that the guilt weight exceeds 0.5, which makes the exercise a parametrisation rather than a calibration, and of the four games analysed in the 1999 paper they say only one arguably beats a money-maximising model. Fehr and Schmidt replied in the same issue. Charness and Rabin ran distribution games built to separate the motives, and found few subjects would pay to reduce inequality by lowering another player's payoff, with Pareto-damaging choices more common when they increased inequality than when they reduced it. Dirk Engelmann and Martin Strobel report that a mix of efficiency concern, maximin preference and selfishness fits their distribution data better than either fairness model. Henrich and colleagues' own figures do not quite agree with each other: their text gives the range of group means as 26% to 58%, while their Table 2 lists Lamalera at 0.57 and Quichua at 0.25.
misreadings: Humans rejecting unfair offers, humans modelled as having inequity-averse preferences, and a monkey throwing cucumber are three claims, and evidence for one is not evidence for another. Henrich made the point in Nature: applied to the capuchin setup, the Fehr-Schmidt model predicts the monkey should eat the cucumber, because refusing it widens the gap rather than closing it, and the grape-eating capuchin sometimes reached through and took the discarded slice. Henrich also noted the human comparison. In an impunity game, where rejection costs the responder but leaves the proposer's payoff untouched, subjects never rejected. Wynne, reading Brosnan and de Waal's own data, reported 43% refusals in the inequality test against 49% in the food control, where a grape sat in the empty partner seat and no second monkey was present. Brosnan and de Waal answered that the levels are not the point and the trends differ, reporting a comparison of regression slopes across trials at F(2,69) = 28.71, p < 0.001. Bräuer, Call and Tomasello added controls and got the opposite pattern in apes, who ignored fewer food pieces when a conspecific received the better food, which they read as expectation of food rather than as fairness. Roma and colleagues found witness rejections infrequent and unrelated to what the other monkey received. The cross-cultural data also undercut the claim that everyone rejects unfair offers: Machiguenga responders rejected once, and the Kazakh, Quichua, Aché and Tsimane rejected nothing at all.
